## Continuous and discrete

- **Continuous signal**: a value at every instant.
- **Discrete signal**: values only at the sample times.
- **Sample index** `n`: which sample, starting at 0.
- **Sample time** `t`: the real time that sample was taken at.
- **Amplitude** `x[n]`: the height of the sample.

actions.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n = np.arange(8)  # sample index starts at 0
t = 0.5 * n  # a 0.5 s sample interval turns the index into time
x = np.array([0, 1, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -1])  # the amplitude of each sample

clips.caption: First set up the <c.aqua>sample index</c.aqua>, the <c.aqua>sample time</c.aqua> and the <c.aqua>amplitude</c.aqua>; note that t is the real time of each sample.

actions.text:
print("n =", n)
print("t =", t)
print("x =", x)

clips.caption: Print the three arrays; the next step checks their lengths and how they line up.
Run this cell first and see how the index, time and <c.aqua>amplitude</c.aqua> of the 8 <c.aqua>samples</c.aqua> line up.

Here 8 <c.aqua>samples</c.aqua> stand for one <c.aqua>discrete signal</c.aqua>. n is the <c.aqua>sample index</c.aqua> and t is the sample time. The sample interval is 0.5 s, so the 4th sample sits at 1.5 s.
After running, read the printed arrays and confirm that index, time and <c.aqua>amplitude</c.aqua> line up one to one.
